title: Burr hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma
subtitle: Wash out, drain, prevent recurrence

sources.org: Santarius T et al, The Lancet
sources.title: Use of drains versus no drains after burr-hole evacuation of chronic subdural haematoma: a randomised controlled trial (Lancet 2009;374:1067-73)

sources.org: Hutchinson PJ et al, N Engl J Med (Dex-CSDH)
sources.title: Trial of dexamethasone for chronic subdural hematoma (N Engl J Med 2020;383:2616-27)

indications: Symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma: headache, confusion, gait disturbance, limb weakness, dysphasia or falling GCS, with a hypodense or mixed-density collection on CT.
Collection with mass effect causing neurological deficit.
Recurrent collection after previous drainage when symptoms return.
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia: correct first unless the patient is deteriorating rapidly.
A small asymptomatic collection, which can be observed.
An acute, hyperdense, clotted subdural, which usually needs a craniotomy rather than burr holes.
preparation: CT within the admission; review the side, the thickest point, membranes and any acute component.
Stop or reverse anticoagulants and antiplatelets per local protocol, and document the plan for restarting.
Do not give routine dexamethasone: in the Dex-CSDH trial it led to fewer favourable outcomes than placebo.
Consent should include recurrence, seizures, infection, acute haemorrhage, stroke, pneumocephalus and the need for further surgery.
positioning: Supine with a sandbag under the shoulder and the head turned to the opposite side, on a horseshoe or head ring.
Keep the head slightly up to reduce venous congestion, without kinking the neck.
Local anaesthesia with sedation is an option for frail patients; general anaesthesia otherwise.
equipment: Cranial perforator and burrs, bone wax, bipolar diathermy.
Soft subdural or subgaleal drain with a closed drainage bag.
Warmed irrigation fluid and a soft catheter for irrigation.
anatomy: The chronic subdural lies between the dura and the arachnoid, contained by an outer and an inner membrane formed by the body's attempt to absorb it.
Bridging veins cross the subdural space from cortex to the venous sinuses. Brain atrophy stretches them, which is why older patients and those on antithrombotics are at risk.
Typical burr hole sites are parietal over the parietal eminence and frontal anterior to the coronal suture, adjusted to the collection on CT.
The middle meningeal artery runs under the pterion and is the vessel targeted by embolisation as an adjunct in recurrent cases.
criticalSafety: Confirm the side from the scan in theatre. Bilateral collections need a decision about which side, or both.
Do not breach the inner membrane or the arachnoid. The cortex lies directly beneath.
Place the drain gently along the inner surface of the dura, not into the brain.
structuresAtRisk: Superior sagittal sinus with a frontal burr hole placed too medially
Middle meningeal artery near the pterion
commonErrors: Placing the burr hole on the wrong side because a bilateral or isodense collection was misread.
Aggressive suction or catheter passage that injures the cortex.
Not placing a drain, which was associated with substantially higher recurrence in trial evidence.
Mobilising the patient too early with an open drain, causing pneumocephalus or overdrainage.
complications: Acute subdural or intracerebral haemorrhage, and seizures.
Post-operative confusion and medical complications in a frail population.
postop: Neurological observations with a written trigger for CT.
Drain left in for a defined period per local practice, usually about 48 hours, and removed when output falls.
Restart antithrombotics on an agreed date balanced against the indication.
Early mobilisation after drain removal, with falls assessment and outpatient follow-up.

steps.emphasis: Check for bilateral collections and confirm which side is being drained.
Head turned with the burr hole site uppermost; avoid neck kinking, which raises venous pressure.
Plan the burr holes over the thickest part of the collection, avoiding the midline.
Open the dura and the outer membrane; dark motor-oil fluid under pressure confirms the diagnosis.
A subdural or subgaleal drain reduces recurrence. Keep the bag below head level, per local practice.

step.csdh.irrigation.title: Irrigation of the subdural space
step.csdh.irrigation.why: Washing out the liquefied haematoma removes the fluid and the inflammatory mediators that drive re-accumulation, while warm irrigation reduces the risk of new bleeding.
how: Irrigate gently with warmed fluid through the burr hole, using a soft catheter directed along the inner surface of the dura.
Continue until the return is clear or nearly clear.
Fill the subdural space with fluid before closing to reduce trapped air.
pitfalls: Directing the catheter towards the brain rather than along the dura.
High-pressure irrigation that tears membranes or veins.
